title: Migraine attack: warning signs, aura, headache
description: A migraine attack is far more than a headache. It unfolds in phases over hours to days: early warning signs such as tiredness and yawning, in some people a visual aura, then the headache with its sensitivity to light and sound, and a washed-out period afterwards. The episode follows the brain through those phases in someone who has migraine. Many attacks have no aura, and not everyone has every phase.
caveat: Each phase here comes from a different small study: eight people whose attacks were set off with a drug, three people scanned during a visual aura, people scanned during spontaneous attacks, and one person scanned every morning for a month. They were never one experiment, and the order of the phases is the clinical one, not something timed in a single brain. An aura occurs in only about a third of people with migraine. The brainstem is drawn as a rough outline of the whole structure: the findings are for small areas inside it. The headache itself is carried by nerve pathways from the coverings of the brain and its blood vessels, which are not part of the brain model. The pain-free finding in the last phase comes from attacks stopped with medication, and what the brain does in the day or two after an untreated attack was not covered by the sources read.

phases.name: Warning signs
phases.timescale: hours to days before the pain
phases.caption: Before any pain: tiredness and yawning. The hypothalamus, which regulates sleep, appetite and body rhythms, becomes more active, along with parts of the brainstem and the visual cortex.

phases.name: Aura
phases.timescale: minutes (in about a third of people)
phases.caption: In about a third of people with migraine, some attacks bring an aura: shimmering zigzags that drift across vision. A wave of raised signal creeps across the visual cortex at a few millimetres a minute, and the signal then diminishes along the same path.

order.rationale: The sequence of phases is the clinical one given in reviews. The aura study recorded the wave across the visual cortex minute by minute, but no study read here followed one person from warning signs through aura to headache.

phases.name: Headache
phases.caption: The headache, with light and sound hard to bear. Blood flow rises in the brainstem and in visual and hearing areas of the cortex, and the hypothalamus and brainstem change how they work together.

order.rationale: The sequence of phases is the clinical one given in reviews. The scans of the headache phase were not taken in the same people as the scans of the earlier phases.

phases.name: After the pain
phases.caption: The pain lifts. In attacks stopped with medication, the brainstem was still active after the headache and the sensitivity to light and sound had gone. What happens in the washed-out day after an untreated attack was not covered by the sources read.

order.rationale: The only brain finding here is from attacks ended by a drug. The gradual return to rest that is drawn is an assumption.

regions.explanation: More active in the warning phase, before any pain, in eight people whose attacks were set off with a drug. In one person scanned daily for a month, its response to a painful stimulus grew over the day before each attack. It is drawn only for the warning phase, because the sources read do not say what its activity does afterwards; its working relationship with the brainstem is reported as altered during the pain.

citations.quote: We found activations in the posterolateral hypothalamus, midbrain tegmental area, periaqueductal grey, dorsal pons and various cortical areas including occipital, temporal and prefrontal cortex.

citations.title: The migraine generator revisited: continuous scanning of the migraine cycle over 30 days and three spontaneous attacks.
citations.quote: hypothalamic activity as a response to trigeminal nociceptive stimulation is altered during the 24 h prior to pain onset, i.e. increases towards the next migraine attack

citations.title: The migraine generator revisited: continuous scanning of the migraine cycle over 30 days and three spontaneous attacks.
citations.quote: the hypothalamus shows altered functional coupling with the spinal trigeminal nuclei and the region of the migraine generator, i.e. the dorsal rostral pons during the preictal day and the pain phase of native human migraine attacks

citations.title: A Phase-by-Phase Review of Migraine Pathophysiology.
citations.quote: The premonitory phase begins as early as 3 days before the headache phase, and involves a complex interplay between various cortical and subcortical brain regions, including the hypothalamus and brainstem nuclei that modulate nociceptive signaling.

regions.explanation: Parts of the brainstem are more active in the warning phase and during the headache. During spontaneous attacks blood flow in the brainstem was raised, and it stayed raised after medication had removed the pain, which is why the brainstem has been called a possible generator of attacks; that idea is disputed. The findings are for small areas inside the brainstem, not all of it. Nothing is drawn during the aura, which the sources read do not cover for the brainstem; the finding after the pain was made straight after medication, not hours later.

regions.explanation: Active in the warning phase, in one small study. During a visual aura, recorded almost continuously in three people, activity rose in one visual area, spread slowly across the visual cortex in step with what the person saw, and then diminished. During the headache, blood flow was raised in visual association cortex. The whole visual cortex is drawn rising and falling together; the real change is a wave moving across it, which this brain model cannot show. The area where the wave began and the visual association areas lie at least partly outside the gyri drawn here.

citations.title: Mechanisms of migraine aura revealed by functional MRI in human visual cortex.
citations.quote: Following the same retinotopic progression, the BOLD signal then diminished (possibly reflecting vasoconstriction after the initial vasodilation), as did the BOLD response to visual activation.
